title: Working with numbers in various contexts

lessons.title: Whole numbers and the four operations at work
lessons.html:
Numbers are everywhere on the farm

Every day on a farm we use numbers. We count chickens in a house, eggs in a tray, bags of feed in the store and crates on the bakkie. We read numbers on a scale, a thermometer and a water meter. Being sure with numbers helps you do your work well and check that you are paid correctly.

Reading and writing big numbers

In South Africa we write big numbers with a space between groups of three digits: 25 000 chickens, R12 500. Read the groups from left to right: "twenty-five thousand". The place of a digit gives its value. In 3 482, the 3 means three thousand, the 4 means four hundred, the 8 means eighty and the 2 means two.

The four operations

  • Adding (+) – putting amounts together. House 1 has 12 400 birds and House 2 has 11 900 birds. Together: 12 400 + 11 900 = 24 300 birds.
  • Subtracting (−) – taking away or finding a difference. A house started with 20 000 chicks and 350 died. 20 000 − 350 = 19 650 birds left.
  • Multiplying (×) – adding the same amount many times. One egg tray holds 30 eggs. 40 trays hold 40 × 30 = 1 200 eggs.
  • Dividing (÷) – sharing equally or finding how many groups. 1 500 eggs ÷ 30 eggs per tray = 50 trays.

Order matters

When a sum has more than one step, do what is inside brackets first, then multiply and divide, then add and subtract. For example, 5 + 3 × 10 = 5 + 30 = 35, not 80. If you mean "5 plus 3, then times 10", write (5 + 3) × 10 = 80.

Using a calculator

A calculator on your phone is a good tool, but you must still think. Type carefully and look at the answer. Ask yourself: does this answer make sense? If you divide 1 500 eggs into trays of 30 and the calculator says 4 500, you pressed the wrong button.

lessons.title: Fractions, decimals and percentages
lessons.html:
Parts of a whole

Often we work with parts, not whole things. Half a bag of feed, a quarter of the field, 10% discount. These are all ways to show part of a whole.

Fractions

A fraction has a top number and a bottom number. In ¾ the bottom number (4) tells how many equal parts the whole is cut into. The top number (3) tells how many parts we have. If a 50 kg feed bag is ¾ full, it holds ¾ of 50 kg. Work it out: 50 ÷ 4 = 12,5, then 12,5 × 3 = 37,5 kg.

Decimals

Decimals are another way to write parts. In South Africa we use a decimal comma: 2,5 kg means two and a half kilograms. Money uses decimals too: R14,50 means 14 rand and 50 cents. Half = 0,5; a quarter = 0,25; three quarters = 0,75.

Percentages

Per cent (%) means "out of 100". 50% is the same as half. 25% is a quarter. 10% is one tenth.

  • To find 10% of an amount, divide by 10. 10% of R3 000 = R300.
  • To find 5%, find 10% and halve it. 5% of R3 000 = R150.
  • To find any percentage, multiply by the percentage and divide by 100. 8% of R4 500 = 4 500 × 8 ÷ 100 = R360.

A farm example: mortality percentage

A broiler house received 20 000 chicks and 400 died during the cycle. What percentage died? Divide the number dead by the number placed, then multiply by 100: 400 ÷ 20 000 × 100 = 2%. Managers use this number to compare one cycle with another.

A pay example

Your wage is R4 000 a month and you get a 6% increase. 6% of R4 000 = R240. Your new wage is R4 000 + R240 = R4 240.

lessons.title: Ratios, rates and checking your answers
lessons.html:
Ratios: comparing amounts

A ratio compares two or more amounts. A common concrete mix on the farm is 1 : 2 : 3 – one part cement, two parts sand, three parts stone. If you use 2 wheelbarrows of cement, you need 2 × 2 = 4 barrows of sand and 2 × 3 = 6 barrows of stone. The ratio stays the same; only the size changes.

When you mix any product, for example a disinfectant, the label gives the mixing ratio. Always measure exactly as the label says. Do not guess and do not "add a bit extra to make it stronger". A wrong mix can harm people, animals or the product's work.

Rates: one thing per another

A rate tells how much of something per one unit of another thing.

  • Pay rate: R30 per hour. 8 hours × R30 = R240 for the day.
  • Speed: the tractor moves 10 km per hour.
  • Price per unit: a 50 kg bag costs R450, so 1 kg costs R450 ÷ 50 = R9.

Best buy

Shop A sells 10 kg maize meal for R95. Shop B sells 5 kg for R52. Price per kg at A: R95 ÷ 10 = R9,50. At B: R52 ÷ 5 = R10,40. Shop A is the better buy, if you can use the bigger bag before it goes off.

Estimating and checking

Before you work out an exact answer, make a quick guess by rounding. 49 bags × R452 is about 50 × R450 = R22 500. If your calculator later says R2 214, you know something is wrong.

Ways to check an answer:

  1. Round the numbers and estimate.
  2. Do the opposite operation. If 1 200 ÷ 30 = 40, then 40 × 30 should give 1 200.
  3. Ask: is the answer sensible? A worker cannot work 30 hours in one day.

Key points

  • Use the four operations (+, −, ×, ÷) to solve everyday farm problems.
  • Do brackets first, then × and ÷, then + and −.
  • Per cent means out of 100; 10% of an amount is the amount divided by 10.
  • Ratios keep the same proportion when you make a bigger or smaller mix.
  • Always estimate and check that your answer makes sense.
